proposal.title: CAP / London 3 — Protected product programme and partner delivery
proposal.reason: Give Alex operational freedom while protecting separately budgeted CP/M TUI, AION C IDE, Abacus and BPI engineering work. Preserve current DRI ownership and AION reuse rights; the acquisition does not renegotiate those terms. Preserve BPI independence and its 1977 agreement. Existing technical product specifications remain authoritative.

before.title: Logix–DRI–AION CP/M, TUI and developer-platform agreement

party.role: Aurelia platform partner and development collaborator
CP/M developer, sole software owner and licensor
negotiator for the Logix collaboration
TUI developer and source-delivery partner; owner and developer of AION C IDE

before.description: Logix, DRI and AION Software agree the Aurelia operating-system and developer platform. DRI develops the CP/M extensions and integrates the TUI implementation delivered by AION. Logix supplies hardware, boot firmware and low-level drivers; AION Labs supplies qualified ROM chips to Logix requirements. AION develops and owns the separate AION C IDE. The January 1975 agreement establishes development obligations; integration and qualification precede the June 1978 launch.

clauses.statement: DRI retains the right to implement the TUI libraries and FlexiBUS support in CP/M versions for non-Logix computers.

DRI leads CP/M command/file services, operating-system memory and cartridge runtime, shared clipboard storage and bounded I/O scheduling. Logix supplies hardware requirements, boot/recovery firmware, initial mapping and low-level drivers. AION Software develops the TUI and the separate C development environment. Logix leads complete-system acceptance with DRI and AION component qualification.

DRI owns the resulting CP/M version, its CP/M enhancements and the accepted CP/M TUI implementation delivered by AION, with source, documentation and tests. DRI may maintain, modify and license these implementations non-exclusively for other hosts. AION retains its compiler/IDE and pre-existing general-purpose components; any such components included in the delivery carry perpetual rights for DRI to maintain, modify and redistribute them with CP/M. Hardware ownership is not transferred.

AION Software designs and implements the shared text-mode TUI API, controls, editing, menus, forms, lists and pseudo-windows, with C bindings and assembly implementations where appropriate. DRI accepts the source and tests and integrates the implementation into the CP/M system cartridge. Mutable state remains in reserved RAM; applications call shared services rather than embedding another full TUI library.
Support smart devices and expansion cards using Plug and Execute and FlexiBUS technologies, with documented CP/M integration so qualified devices and cards can expose their functions to applications.

DRI adapts CP/M and suitable cartridge code for XIP, separating ROM code/constants from RAM state. Logix supplies mapping hardware and safe boot primitives. Define image headers, entry points, relocation assumptions, RAM initialization, nested calls, callbacks and recovery. Arbitrary existing CP/M binaries are not automatically ROM-executable.

DRI implements user-area support and named groups as explicit extensions to the CP/M 1.4-derived release. Names map to CP/M User Numbers; they do not create hierarchical directories. DRI specifies persistent name metadata, valid names, default selection, enumeration, rename behaviour and compatibility with ordinary CP/M tools before interface freeze.

Logix, DRI and AION jointly maintain the published TUI interface specification. AION retains perpetual rights to reuse, modify and port the delivered TUI source and shared technology for other operating systems and processors, including non-CP/M targets. DRI retains independent CP/M licensing; later improvements require documented compatibility and contribution terms rather than an implied transfer of unrelated software.

DRI owns operating-system bank and cartridge dispatch, preserves caller mappings and stacks, and handles nested calls, interrupts and page-crossing buffers. Stable common-memory code and the system stack remain accessible. Logix owns reset mapping, hardware primitives and controller timing/refresh/DMA behaviour. Installed RAM is distinct from the writable application area advertised before launch; no service silently reduces a running application's TPA.

Logix supplies hardware video drivers and monitor capability discovery. DRI integrates mode selection and supported display services into CP/M, rejecting unsupported configurations. AION implements adaptive TUI layout and rendering over those services, without assuming fixed video addresses or universal 80-column support.

DRI provides clipboard storage/lifecycle and a bounded I/O request service. AION and DRI define clipboard formats and copy/cut/paste semantics. Clipboard and I/O buffers have separate lifetimes and ownership. Define bounds, overflow, persistence, per-device ordering, completion, cancellation, timeouts, errors and flushing; slow devices must not block keyboard service. Standard CP/M calls retain synchronous semantics; this does not introduce foreground multitasking.

Logix owns hardware and cartridge electrical design, address decode and ROM capacity/timing requirements. AION Labs implements and manufactures qualified ROM chips to those requirements under Logix supply arrangements. DRI releases the integrated CP/M image after accepting AION TUI source; Logix controls production image revisions, programming/mask handover and verification with AION Labs. Semiconductor manufacture transfers no software rights.

AION Software develops and owns AION C IDE for Aurelia: integrated editor/build workflow, Z80 C compiler and optimizer, assembler/linker, runtime libraries, TUI bindings, diagnostics, debugging and disk/XIP image tools. The IDE is a separately distributed disk-based offering; the reusable TUI runtime is supplied in the CP/M system cartridge. DRI supplies stable OS interfaces and integration assistance.

Agree interface and calling-convention freezes, source/test/documentation handovers, component acceptance and complete-system qualification before the June 1978 release. DRI funds/staffs its OS work, AION its TUI/IDE work and Logix its platform/integration work, subject to separately documented commercial arrangements. Assign defect ownership by component and jointly triage integration faults. Measure ROM images, stacks, buffers and application RAM; publish supported configurations and replacement/patch procedures. No date alone proves acceptance or manufacturing readiness.

before.title: Aurelia Foundation and Partnerships
before.description: Establish the commercial and partnership foundation for Aurelia: CP/M implementation, independent BPI cooperation, printer-mechanism supply, ComputerLand distribution and Academy support. Include the Aurelia launch campaign, NCC presentations, the start of BPI training and the dealer programme through the campaign’s end on 17 July 1978. The campaign hierarchy also owns recording, editing and free television distribution of cleared NCC material.

inputs.description: The established DRI partnership enables the Aurelia CP/M implementation agreement that starts this process.
Logix and AION provide the product, engineering and distribution organisation needed to negotiate and carry out the Aurelia partnerships.

outcomes.description: Aurelia has a partnership foundation covering CP/M implementation, OEM printer mechanisms, ComputerLand distribution and Academy support, as documented in the constituent events.

BPI pilot testing, launch qualification and dealer/instructor preparation support the launch of its independently owned Aurelia applications. Qualification gates and support limits remain those recorded in the milestones; BPI has accepted Adam’s investment and AION’s C/TUI redevelopment obligations, with future-platform work and a subsequent BPI share-buyback right.

steps.description: BPI accepts the investment and C/TUI redevelopment agreement.
OEM printer-mechanism agreement.
ComputerLand retail agreement.
BPI business and accountant pilot programme.
Establish and prepare Logix Computer Academy through its dedicated launch-and-training process, from its founding event through 17 July 1978.
BPI and AION engineers tested the application family with businesses and accounting practices, reconciling its reports with existing records.
The partners checked posting, corrections, backup recovery, advertised payroll coverage and the summary export to Abacus.
BPI trained dealers and Academy instructors in the released configurations and its specialist-support arrangements before the June launch.

Run the Aurelia launch and Academy campaign through NCC presentations and the combined BPI training and dealer-programme opening on 17 July 1978. Prepare follow-up plans; completion of this campaign also completes the foundation process.
Coordinate the marketing campaign: Aurelia 1978 launch campaign and Logix Computer Academy.

before.title: BPI investment, redevelopment, distribution and training agreement

party.role: investor receiving a 33% fully diluted interest
accepting company and software owner
committed redevelopment and porting partner
distribution and training
BPI-authorised practical training and direct distribution provider

before.description: BPI Systems accepts Adam’s $150,000 investment in exchange for a 33% fully diluted interest. The agreement obliges AION Software to provide knowledge and resources to refactor BPI’s existing code into C with a competitive text-mode TUI. Further investment supports ports to future systems and platforms, after which BPI has the right to buy back Adam’s shares. The same agreement covers BPI’s operating independence, distribution, specialist support and authorised training. Logix and the Academy provide distribution, hardware support and training services.

clauses.statement: Adam agrees to subscribe $150,000 of new capital into BPI Systems for development and working capital. BPI accepts the subscription; it is company funding rather than a payment to existing owners.

The accepted investment agreement allocates Adam a 33% fully diluted interest in BPI Systems in exchange for his $150,000 subscription. Existing owners retain the remaining 67%, subject to the agreed later buyback right.
clauses.unit: percent of BPI fully diluted shares

clauses.statement: AION Software must provide the knowledge, engineering resources and development assistance needed to refactor BPI’s current code into C and deliver a competitive TUI with pseudo-window interaction in text mode. BPI retains ownership of its applications and its independent brand and management.

The cooperation includes further investment and engineering work to port the refactored BPI software to future systems and platforms. AION Software supplies the associated technical knowledge and resources. Additional funding amounts, allocation among contributors, target platforms and schedules remain unspecified.

Following the agreed redevelopment and subsequent porting work, BPI Systems may buy back Adam’s shares. This is BPI’s right, not an automatic transfer or a mandatory buyback. The agreement does not specify a price, valuation formula, exercise date or payment schedule.

BPI retained its management, brand, application ownership, licensing and specialist support. AION Software provided engineering assistance and Logix provided distribution and training. Operational cooperation implements the accepted investment and C/TUI redevelopment agreement while preserving BPI’s operating independence.

BPI owned its applications and managed licensing, updates and specialist support. AION Software supplied engineering assistance, while Logix distributed the products and supported the hardware. Dealers handled installation enquiries. Public presentations described this commercial partnership and identified Adam’s accepted investment and the C/TUI redevelopment partnership.

Academy begins BPI-authorised practical courses and direct distribution under a cooperation agreement. Dealers handle first-line installation enquiries, BPI handles software defects and specialist support, and Logix supports hardware. Tuition, setup services and software licences remain separate.

clauses.statement: DRI retains the right to implement the TUI libraries and FlexiBUS support in CP/M versions for non-Logix computers.

DRI leads CP/M command/file services, operating-system memory and cartridge runtime, shared clipboard storage and bounded I/O scheduling. Logix supplies hardware requirements, boot/recovery firmware, initial mapping and low-level drivers. AION Software develops the TUI and the separate C development environment. Logix leads complete-system acceptance with DRI and AION component qualification.

DRI owns the resulting CP/M version, its CP/M enhancements and the accepted CP/M TUI implementation delivered by AION, with source, documentation and tests. DRI may maintain, modify and license these implementations non-exclusively for other hosts. AION retains its compiler/IDE and pre-existing general-purpose components; any such components included in the delivery carry perpetual rights for DRI to maintain, modify and redistribute them with CP/M. Hardware ownership is not transferred.

AION Software designs and implements the shared text-mode TUI API, controls, editing, menus, forms, lists and pseudo-windows, with C bindings and assembly implementations where appropriate. DRI accepts the source and tests and integrates the implementation into the CP/M system cartridge. Mutable state remains in reserved RAM; applications call shared services rather than embedding another full TUI library.
Support smart devices and expansion cards using Plug and Execute and FlexiBUS technologies, with documented CP/M integration so qualified devices and cards can expose their functions to applications.

DRI adapts CP/M and suitable cartridge code for XIP, separating ROM code/constants from RAM state. Logix supplies mapping hardware and safe boot primitives. Define image headers, entry points, relocation assumptions, RAM initialization, nested calls, callbacks and recovery. Arbitrary existing CP/M binaries are not automatically ROM-executable.

DRI implements user-area support and named groups as explicit extensions to the CP/M 1.4-derived release. Names map to CP/M User Numbers; they do not create hierarchical directories. DRI specifies persistent name metadata, valid names, default selection, enumeration, rename behaviour and compatibility with ordinary CP/M tools before interface freeze.

Logix, DRI and AION jointly maintain the published TUI interface specification. AION retains perpetual rights to reuse, modify and port the delivered TUI source and shared technology for other operating systems and processors, including non-CP/M targets. DRI retains independent CP/M licensing; later improvements require documented compatibility and contribution terms rather than an implied transfer of unrelated software.

DRI owns operating-system bank and cartridge dispatch, preserves caller mappings and stacks, and handles nested calls, interrupts and page-crossing buffers. Stable common-memory code and the system stack remain accessible. Logix owns reset mapping, hardware primitives and controller timing/refresh/DMA behaviour. Installed RAM is distinct from the writable application area advertised before launch; no service silently reduces a running application's TPA.

Logix supplies hardware video drivers and monitor capability discovery. DRI integrates mode selection and supported display services into CP/M, rejecting unsupported configurations. AION implements adaptive TUI layout and rendering over those services, without assuming fixed video addresses or universal 80-column support.

DRI provides clipboard storage/lifecycle and a bounded I/O request service. AION and DRI define clipboard formats and copy/cut/paste semantics. Clipboard and I/O buffers have separate lifetimes and ownership. Define bounds, overflow, persistence, per-device ordering, completion, cancellation, timeouts, errors and flushing; slow devices must not block keyboard service. Standard CP/M calls retain synchronous semantics; this does not introduce foreground multitasking.

Logix owns hardware and cartridge electrical design, address decode and ROM capacity/timing requirements. AION Labs implements and manufactures qualified ROM chips to those requirements under Logix supply arrangements. DRI releases the integrated CP/M image after accepting AION TUI source; Logix controls production image revisions, programming/mask handover and verification with AION Labs. Semiconductor manufacture transfers no software rights.

AION Software develops and owns AION C IDE for Aurelia: integrated editor/build workflow, Z80 C compiler and optimizer, assembler/linker, runtime libraries, TUI bindings, diagnostics, debugging and disk/XIP image tools. The IDE is a separately distributed disk-based offering; the reusable TUI runtime is supplied in the CP/M system cartridge. DRI supplies stable OS interfaces and integration assistance.

Agree interface and calling-convention freezes, source/test/documentation handovers, component acceptance and complete-system qualification before the June 1978 release. DRI funds/staffs its OS work, AION its TUI/IDE work and Logix its platform/integration work, subject to separately documented commercial arrangements. Assign defect ownership by component and jointly triage integration faults. Measure ROM images, stacks, buffers and application RAM; publish supported configurations and replacement/patch procedures. No date alone proves acceptance or manufacturing readiness.

AION Software assigns named technical leads, staffing, budgets and component milestones to TUI and C IDE delivery. Alex protects this capacity alongside existing customer contracts and other initiatives. Develop interfaces and reference implementations first, then the compiler, assembler/linker, editor and runtime, with staged optimisation and integration qualification. Existing agreement terms govern DRI ownership of accepted CP/M TUI delivery and AION’s perpetual reuse rights.

before.description: BPI Systems accepts Adam’s $150,000 investment in exchange for a 33% fully diluted interest. The agreement obliges AION Software to provide knowledge and resources to refactor BPI’s existing code into C with a competitive text-mode TUI. Further investment supports ports to future systems and platforms, after which BPI has the right to buy back Adam’s shares. The same agreement covers BPI’s operating independence, distribution, specialist support and authorised training. Logix and the Academy provide distribution, hardware support and training services.

clauses.statement: Adam agrees to subscribe $150,000 of new capital into BPI Systems for development and working capital. BPI accepts the subscription; it is company funding rather than a payment to existing owners.

The accepted investment agreement allocates Adam a 33% fully diluted interest in BPI Systems in exchange for his $150,000 subscription. Existing owners retain the remaining 67%, subject to the agreed later buyback right.
clauses.unit: percent of BPI fully diluted shares

clauses.statement: AION Software must provide the knowledge, engineering resources and development assistance needed to refactor BPI’s current code into C and deliver a competitive TUI with pseudo-window interaction in text mode. BPI retains ownership of its applications and its independent brand and management.

The cooperation includes further investment and engineering work to port the refactored BPI software to future systems and platforms. AION Software supplies the associated technical knowledge and resources. Additional funding amounts, allocation among contributors, target platforms and schedules remain unspecified.

Following the agreed redevelopment and subsequent porting work, BPI Systems may buy back Adam’s shares. This is BPI’s right, not an automatic transfer or a mandatory buyback. The agreement does not specify a price, valuation formula, exercise date or payment schedule.

BPI retained its management, brand, application ownership, licensing and specialist support. AION Software provided engineering assistance and Logix provided distribution and training. Operational cooperation implements the accepted investment and C/TUI redevelopment agreement while preserving BPI’s operating independence.

BPI owned its applications and managed licensing, updates and specialist support. AION Software supplied engineering assistance, while Logix distributed the products and supported the hardware. Dealers handled installation enquiries. Public presentations described this commercial partnership and identified Adam’s accepted investment and the C/TUI redevelopment partnership.

Academy begins BPI-authorised practical courses and direct distribution under a cooperation agreement. Dealers handle first-line installation enquiries, BPI handles software defects and specialist support, and Logix supports hardware. Tuition, setup services and software licences remain separate.
